about: The geometry kernel's quality ledger (kernel architecture 28.8). survivors: every mutant cargo-mutants makes that the kernel's tests do not catch and the kernel keeps, keyed by file, cargo-mutants' description and the trimmed text of the mutated line, with why; in the foundation set only equivalent mutants (no input through the crate's public interface can tell them from the original) may be kept. coverage_off: every coverage(off) mark in a kernel crate, with the Kani or Verus proof that the code it hides cannot run. awaiting_proof: every foundation line the tests do not run yet, by its file, its trimmed text and how many missed lines have it, with the piece that proves it unreachable or tests it (the coverage gate landed before those proofs: owner decision of 2026-10-27); the list can only shrink. geom-test's kernel-quality binary checks both in .github/workflows/kernel-quality.yml; geom_test::quality_ledger documents the format.

survivors.reason: row_pair is pub(crate), and its three callers pass two different rows inside the matrix: Lu::factor rows k < i < n, canonical_null_space row and i with i != row, both below d, and swap_rows only after returning early when i == j. survivors.line_text: .fold(0.0f64, |m, v| if v.abs() > m { v.abs() } else { m });
survivors.reason: The fold keeps the largest magnitude. The mutant takes v.abs() also when it equals m, which is the same double (finite entries, never NaN, and an absolute value is never -0), so the scale, and every norm, is the same.

tau has min(m, n) entries. The mutant also reads entry (k, k) for k = min(m, n), but the matrix has no such entry (k is at least its row or its column count), so get refuses it and .ok() gives None, as the original does.

survivors.mutant: replace > with >= in <impl MaxZero for f64>::max_zero
survivors.reason: max_zero's one caller passes 1.0 - r * r. The two versions differ only for self = 0 or -0, where the mutant returns self; a difference of doubles is -0 only when both are zeros of opposite sign, and 1.0 is not zero, so self is never -0 and +0 is returned either way.

The mutant also enters the block when rank == n. Each row's reflection is then on the one coordinate k: householder on a one-entry vector finds a zero tail and returns tau = 0 and beta = the entry, so R(k, k) is set to itself, z_tau keeps its zeros and no row is updated; apply_z returns early when r == n. The work was charged before.

The mutant pivots on the last of several rows of equal largest magnitude instead of the first. The reduced echelon basis over the variable order is unique (chapter 15.8, the reason it is the canonical one), so the result is the same basis either way; the elimination order changes only the rounding of its entries, which the function does not promise bit for bit.

abs is private, and every caller uses what it returns only in a comparison: fast_two_sum compares abs(b) > abs(a), split compares abs(a) < 2^996, two_prod compares abs(p), abs(a) and abs(b) with powers of two. The mutant changes the result only for x = +0 or -0, where it returns the other zero, and -0 and +0 compare equal in every comparison, so no public function's result changes.

x.to_bits() & !EXPONENT_BITS clears every exponent bit, and ONE_BITS, the bits of 1.0, has only exponent bits set (field 1023, no sign, no fraction). Two words with no set bit in common give the same word under OR and XOR, so unit_binade returns the same double for every x.

survivors.line_text: let (larger, smaller) = if abs(b) > abs(a) { (b, a) } else { (a, b) };
survivors.reason: The mutant also swaps the operands when |a| = |b|. Dekker's step needs only |larger| >= |smaller|, which both orders meet, and IEEE addition is commutative, so s is the same. When a = b the two orders are the same pair; when a = -b, s is +0 and the error smaller + larger is +0 either way; for -0 and +0 the error is -0 or +0, which zero_to_plus makes +0; two infinities of one sign give (s, -s) with s infinite either way, and of opposite signs the invalid sum, a NaN whose bits Rust does not fix (the function documents NaN only as NaN). A NaN input makes both comparisons false, so neither version swaps. Every result is the same.

survivors.line_text: if y < x { y } else { x }
survivors.reason: min2 is private, and its only callers (Interval::mul, div and mul_add) pass what it returns straight to widened(). The mutant answers differently only when x and y are equal: two equal non-zero doubles have the same bits, so either is the same answer; for -0 and +0 it returns the other zero, but widened() takes next_down of the bound, which is -2^-1074 for either zero. Every interval a public operation returns has the same bits.

survivors.line_text: if y > x { y } else { x }
survivors.reason: max2 is private. In Interval::mul, div and mul_add its result goes straight to widened(), which takes next_up of the bound: +2^-1074 for either zero, so returning the other of two equal values (the only change, when x equals y) gives the same bits. Its one other caller, Interval::square's branch for an interval holding zero, passes -lo and hi with lo < 0 < hi, two positive doubles, which are equal only with the same bits.

In this branch (hi <= 0) near and far are used only as near * near, far * far and near == 0.0. IEEE 754 multiplication gives (-a) * (-a) and a * a the same bits (the product of two equal signs is positive, with the same magnitude), and -0.0 == 0.0 is true, so dropping either minus changes no bound that Interval::square, Interval::norm or anything built on them returns.

lo is the literal 0.0 (when the interval holds zero) or zero_to_plus of a rounded square moved down one step, so it is never -0. The mutant differs only when lo equals zero, and then returns the literal 0.0 where the original returns lo, which is +0 too: the same bits in every interval Interval::square returns.

sqrt_nonneg is private and its only caller, Interval::norm, passes it a sum of squares (an empty list returns [0, 0] before reaching it). Interval::square's upper bound is next_up of a non-negative double, at least 2^-1074, and Interval::add's is next_up of a sum of such bounds, so the upper bound reaching sqrt_nonneg is always positive: hi < 0 and hi == 0 are both false for every call, and the mutant changes no result of Interval::norm.

survivors.line_text: let lo = if self.lo < 0.0 { 0.0 } else { self.lo };
survivors.reason: The mutant differs only when the lower bound equals zero, and then passes the literal 0.0 on to Interval::sqrt where the original passes self.lo. Every Interval stores a zero bound as +0 (its invariant: Interval::new, widened() and square apply zero_to_plus or write 0.0), so both are +0 and Interval::norm returns the same bits.

The validity check only skips masks whose matrix has a zero determinant, so weakening it changes no result. A mask that picks two entries of one column sets two rows to the same unit vector, a zero determinant. A mask that picks two entries of one row builds the matrix of a smaller mask (the row keeps one unit vector), which the walk visited earlier and found zero, or which itself repeats a column. Checked by simulating the walk with and without the check on 4,000 random orient2d and incircle ties: every sign agreed.

The mutant also runs the narrowing check when M equals L, a resize to the same width. Then no limb is dropped (skipping M limbs of an L-limb array leaves none, so all() holds) and the copy r has the very limbs of self, so its sign is self's: the check never returns None, and Wide::resize returns the same Some(r) for every value and every pair of widths.

The line runs only inside `if high_a != high_b`, where the two limbs differ, and for different values `<` and `<=` give the same answer, so no input can tell the mutant from the original.

The line runs only for a limb at index L or above. The crate reaches from_magnitude only through product_i128 (checked_mul_i128 has no caller outside the tests), always with four limbs and only at widths 4 and 5: crossing.rs's side::<4> and side::<5>, plane.rs's I256 products and lpi_classify::<4> and ::<5>, and the generated I256 paths. For a negative v the mutant takes the other arm, `v as u128`, which reads v's two's complement as unsigned, v + 2^128: the same u the original builds as (v - i128::MIN) + 2^127 (it only avoids a cast clippy flags as losing the sign). For v = 0 the mutant takes the first arm, where 0 - i128::MIN overflows, so checked_sub gives None and u = 0, as `0 as u128` does. Every v gives the same u, so the same limbs.
The two differ only at v = 0, where the mutant takes the first arm: 0 - i128::MIN = 2^127 overflows i128, so checked_sub gives None and u = 0, the same u as the original's `0 as u128`.
This arm runs for a negative v, where d = v - i128::MIN lies in 0..2^127, so bit 127 of d is clear: setting it with | and flipping it with ^ both give d + 2^127.
Basis::span's binary search goes on at high - low = 1, where mid = low and neither end moves: the loop never ends for a parameter inside a span.
With (high - low) % 2, mid stays at low whenever high - low is even, and a parameter above u_mid then sets low = mid again: Basis::span's binary search never ends.
With == 1 the binary search runs only while high - low is exactly 1, where mid = low and neither end moves, so once it starts it never ends (and a parameter whose search starts there hangs).

survivors.line_text: if b > a { b } else { a }
survivors.reason: The two differ only when b == a, where either is the same number: every caller passes an interval's upper end, a width, a weight or an absolute value, none NaN and none -0 (intervals keep a zero end as +0, and abs gives +0), so equal values have equal bits.

survivors.line_text: if b < a { b } else { a }
survivors.reason: The two differ only when b == a, where either is the same number: every caller passes weights, which are positive, error bounds, which are interval upper ends and never -0, or the starting infinity, so equal values have equal bits.

At r = 0 the block's two loops are empty: r = p - mlt = 0 makes mlt >= p, so mlt + 1..=p is empty, and 1..=r is empty. Its first line, ub - ua in the exact type, cannot fail for the finite knots Basis::new admits, so nothing changes.

At oldr = 1 remove_shared_knot's loop over tr in 1..oldr is empty, and what it does before the loop only reads: first = kind - 2 (kind is past the first piece, so at least q + 1), den = ub - ua > 0 and bet, none of which can fail. Nothing is written.

j - i starts at 2tr and falls by 2, so the extra step comes only for even tr, at i = kind - 1 - tr/2, j = kind - 1 + tr/2, kj = tr/2. There i >= cind = kind - q, as tr/2 < q, so Q is not written; and kj = tr/2 < lbz = oldr/2 + 1, a slot of the piece below lbz that is never copied out and that no later step reads (later steps read kj and kj + 1 above (tr+1)/2).

The two differ only at i == cind, where the mutant writes Q[cind]: the point the copy of the elevated piece (from lbz, never above q) writes first, right after this function returns. No step here reads Q[cind] in between, as i only grows past it.

Bezier extraction takes clamped bases only, whose last p + 1 knots are equal: the scan of the last run always reaches ie = m, and the step after it makes ie = m + 1. So the loop test never sees ie == m, the one value where the two differ.
At mlt == p, r = p - mlt = 0: the loop over mlt + 1..=p and the loop over 1..=r are both empty, and num, an exact difference of two finite knots, cannot fail. Nothing changes.
The two differ only at order == 0, where the right operand is 0 >= degree, false for every basis: Basis::new refuses degree 0. So the test is false either way.

At k = 0 the block rebuilds the net column by column through derivative_points with no levels, which returns the same knots and points (its loop over 1..=k is empty, its finiteness check passes on stored points); the net, rows and knots come out unchanged, and vec_for charges the meter nothing.
At l = 0 the block rebuilds each row through derivative_points with no levels, which returns the same knots and points; the net and knots come out unchanged, and vec_for charges the meter nothing.

A defect check that no input reaches: elevating the reduced basis and inserting the knots it lacks gives back exactly the input's knots (copies of the same doubles) and as many points. Both operands are false, so the test is false with && as with ||.
At r = 0 the block's loops are empty: r = p - mlt = 0 makes mlt >= p, so mlt + 1..=p is empty, and 1..=r is empty. Its first line is ub - ua in doubles, which cannot fail. Nothing changes.

The sweeps write rw at indices 0 to last + 1 - off = p - s + 2 at most (first = r - p, last = r - s, off = first - 1, s >= 1), so at most p + 1 <= 29, and 2 + WIDTH = 31 holds them as 2 * WIDTH does. The buffer is otherwise only read where written.

Both loops differ only when i meets j, which happens when first + last is even, at i = j = (first + last)/2 = (2r - p - s)/2 = fout: the one point remove_once drops from its output. Every extra write (the sweep's, the crossing average, the copy) is to that point, so the result is the same.

A defect check that no input reaches: inserting u back as many times as it was removed gives exactly the input's knots (the same doubles in the same places) and as many points. Both operands are false, so the test is false with && as with ||.

A defect check that no input reaches: re-inserting the removed copy of x once, at x's span from the right with s - 1 copies left, gives back exactly the window's knots (copies of the same doubles in the same places) and one point more than the removal left, as many as the window had. survivors.line_text: if i >= self.n || j >= self.n || add(j, self.lower)? < i || j > add(i, self.upper)? {
survivors.reason: A defect check that no caller reaches: solve reads (i, k) for i from k + 1 to min(k + lower, n - 1) and (k, j) for j up to min(k + upper, n - 1), and solve_rows sets only each row's own entries, whose columns lie within the widths it measured from those rows. All four tests are false, so any && among them is false as the || is.
V1 is the only FitVersion and its number is 1, so returning 1 is what the function does; a second version gets another number, and this mutant then dies.

survivors.line_text: knots.push(if knot > hi { hi } else { knot });
survivors.reason: The two differ only when knot == hi, where both push the same double unless one is +0 and the other -0. That needs hi = -0 and lo + alpha*(0 - lo) to round to 0, so alpha*|lo| to round to |lo|; but alpha = r/den is at most 1 - 1/den, and den, at most the number of parameters, is far below 2^51, so alpha*|lo| rounds below |lo|.

u_1 is +0 for every basis this function gets: curve_parameters starts every parameter list at exactly +0 (0/m for uniform, a pushed 0.0 otherwise), and end_derivative_knots puts p + 1 copies of the first parameter first, p >= 2. So x - 0 and x + 0 are the same double.

survivors.line_text: if rows < 2 || b.len() != mul(rows, width)? || count < 2 || count > rows {
survivors.reason: A defect check whose operands are all false for every caller: curve_parameters refuses fewer than two points, every caller builds b with rows x width values, a basis has at least p + 1 >= 2 functions, and count <= rows is checked first (least_squares_knots refuses more, approximate returns before fitting more). So any && among them is false as the || is.
